implementation_notes: Actuator supplies the structure: health information is collected from a HealthContributorRegistry (each HealthIndicator returns a Health with a Status), a StatusAggregator derives the overall status, and /actuator/health maps DOWN and OUT_OF_SERVICE to 503 while UP stays 200. Health groups split the same registry into dedicated endpoints, and liveness and readiness are auto-configured from the ApplicationAvailability state as /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness (disabled with management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled). Two documented cautions matter operationally: the liveness group must not contain checks on external systems, and a probe answered from a separate management port can succeed while the main server is broken - management.endpoint.health.probes.add-additional-paths=true exposes the groups on the main port as /livez and /readyz. Java has no single answer but two dominant, complete ones: Spring Boot Actuator (a HealthContributorRegistry of HealthIndicators, a StatusAggregator, /actuator/health mapped to 200/503, and liveness/readiness health groups backed by ApplicationAvailability) and MicroProfile Health (annotated HealthCheck procedures exposed at /health/live, /health/ready and /health/started). Both replace the registry, the aggregation and the transport mapping; what remains is the honest assignment of checks to liveness versus readiness and the configuration of probes on the port that actually serves traffic. The classic structure is justified only inside a check that needs its own timeout, cache or circuit breaker.
idiom_name: Spring Boot Actuator /actuator/health plus liveness/readiness groups
pitfalls: Adding a database indicator to the liveness group restarts every instance when the database is unavailable - Boot's own documentation states that the liveness probe must not depend on external systems.
show-details=always publishes dependency internals to every caller; keep it never or when-authorized, or serve the detailed view on an internal port only.

Indicators are invoked per request and Boot warns above ten seconds per indicator, but nothing bounds them: an indicator without a query timeout can exceed the probe deadline and be reported as a dead instance.

variants.name: MicroProfile Health endpoints (@Liveness/@Readiness/@Startup)
variants.implementation_notes: In Jakarta EE / MicroProfile runtimes the same semantics are standardised by the platform: a HealthCheck implementation annotated @Liveness, @Readiness or @Startup is discovered by the container and exposed at /health/live, /health/ready and /health/started, with a combined /health endpoint; each procedure answers HealthCheckResponse.up()/down(), and the overall status of an endpoint is the logical AND of all procedures bound to it. It replaces the hand-written registry, the aggregator and the transport mapping exactly as Actuator does, but with a different wire contract and a much smaller configuration surface - choose it when the runtime is WildFly, Quarkus, Open Liberty or another MicroProfile implementation rather than Spring.
variants.idiom_name: MicroProfile Health 4.0 endpoints with annotated HealthCheck procedures
pitfalls: A HealthCheck implementation without one of the annotations is silently ignored, so a check that never runs looks exactly like a passing endpoint.

Procedures bound to an endpoint are invoked in an unpredictable order and the endpoint is UP only if all of them are - annotating one class with several kinds couples liveness and readiness by accident.

Because the endpoints belong to the runtime, paths and ports come from runtime configuration: if that management listener is not reachable from the orchestrator, the probe measures nothing while looking configured.
